newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: CENTRAL BANK SEES MERGERS ON HORIZON.
newsitem.headline: CENTRAL BANK SEES MERGERS ON HORIZON.

text.p: Lithuania's central bank sees mergers on the horizon as the country's banking sector pulls itself out of a crisis and smaller banks scramble to meet tough new requirements.

"It will be necessary for some banks to look for partners because they are not very competitive and cannot provide a wide range of services," Jonas Niaura, the deputy govenor of the Bank of Lithuania, told Reuters in an interview.
"Specifically, Siauliu Bank and Litimpeks Bank will have to think hard about their future strategies," he added.
The two banks, with 20 million litas and 40.1 million litas respectively in registered share capital at the end of 1996, are among the smallest of the twelve banks currently operating in Lithuania.
Niaura said that smaller banks will have a tough time meeting central bank regulations such as minimum capital requirements, which will gradually be increased each year.
He added that new international accounting standards will give a "clearer picture of what is going on in the banking system."
Niaura said that the larger banks seemed to be in good shape and set to publish good results for 1996.
"Vilniuas Bank, Hermis Bank and the Agriculture Bank should all have profits for 1996," Niaura said.
He also said that some foreign banks were examining the possibility of following the lead of Poland's Kredyt Bank and setting up shop in the Baltic state.
"There are some German and Estonian banks which have looked into the requirements for establishing a branch in Lithuania," Niaura said. "But they have not submitted formal applications."
Niaura said that the sector was shaking off the effects of last year's crisis.
"There is a diminishing amount of bad loans in portfolios...banks are examining risks and assessing their clients carefully," he said.

"Banks are getting more information about their clients," he said, noting that banks now had access to a central data base which lists individuals and companies which have taken out loans exceeding 50,000 litas.
"Without a doubt, the banking system is getting stronger," he said.
He added that the secondary T-bill market, which has been relatively inactive in recent months, was a good sign that the sector was rebounding.
"Banks are not facing liquidity shortages and so they don't need to sell their government paper," he said.
